title: PRIMARY KEY
description: Declare single or composite primary identity with correct MySQL syntax, distinguish key enforcement from automatic numbering, and preserve dependency and data requirements during key changes.
notes:
## A primary key declares the table's designated identity

A PRIMARY KEY constraint identifies the selected complete key for accepted table rows. Under the target rules, key values are unique and every component is required. A campus enrollment table can use the combination student_id and course_id as its designated identity when the model permits only one current accepted enrollment for each pair.

The syntax should follow the model rather than determine it accidentally. A single student can have several courses, so making student_id alone the primary key would reject legitimate enrollments. A course can have many students, so course_id alone is also insufficient. The complete combination expresses the stated row grain, which is the central decision before the keywords are written.

## Single-column and composite declarations differ

A single-column primary key can be declared alongside the column or through the appropriate table-level clause. A composite primary key lists its component columns together in one table-level PRIMARY KEY declaration. Writing PRIMARY KEY separately on both columns does not declare a composite identity; it attempts more than one primary-key declaration.

A table can declare at most one primary-key constraint. That constraint can contain several columns, and the table can have other supported unique rules. SQL can also permit a table with no declared primary key, even though an application design often needs a clear identity. Distinguish the syntax limit from the design recommendation rather than saying every table must declare exactly one.

```sql
CREATE TABLE current_enrollments (
  student_id INT NOT NULL,
  course_id INT NOT NULL,
  PRIMARY KEY (student_id, course_id)
);
```

## The full combination is what must not repeat

Pairs (1,10), (1,20) and (2,10) satisfy the composite rule because each complete pair is different. A second (1,10) conflicts. The repeated components are legitimate and necessary in the many-to-many model. Explain the boundary with these concrete facts so a learner does not confuse a multi-column key with several independent single-column restrictions.

Every component must also be present. A NULL course identifier does not identify a complete enrollment under the stated key contract. Explicit NOT NULL declarations can make that intent readable even when the primary-key definition already imposes required key presence. A key is not a place to encode an unresolved relationship by leaving one identifying component unknown.

## Automatic generation is a separate feature

AUTO_INCREMENT in MySQL supplies values under its supported rules; PRIMARY KEY enforces the designated stored identity. These properties are often paired on one surrogate column, but they are logically distinct. MySQL also has indexing requirements for AUTO_INCREMENT, so logical independence should not be overstated as freedom to ignore every declaration restriction.

PostgreSQL identity and SERIAL mechanisms have their own generation behaviour. A generated number alone is not a universal guarantee of uniqueness, chronology or gapless counting. The key constraint still has a role, and a separate business uniqueness rule may be needed. Generating enrollment_id does not automatically enforce one accepted student-course participation unless the model adds that pair rule too.

## Add a key only to compatible existing data

An ALTER TABLE that adds a primary key makes a claim about the table's current accepted rows. Existing duplicate combinations or missing components must be addressed according to an explicit data policy. A report that simply hides duplicate rows with DISTINCT does not repair the source or establish a suitable ongoing key boundary.

The alteration exercise supplies compatible candidate rows and uses strict mode for the fixture's invalid-write expectations. It does not silently coerce missing identifiers or delete duplicate facts to force success. A real populated transition requires inspection of the actual values and target engine's conversion and validation rules, along with coordination for concurrent writers.

## MySQL uses a special primary-key identifier

MySQL's primary-key index is identified as PRIMARY in the relevant syntax and metadata. Dropping it uses ALTER TABLE table_name DROP PRIMARY KEY rather than assuming an arbitrary CONSTRAINT label becomes a portable removal name. Other products expose their own named constraint rules, so a generic claim that every omitted primary-key name must be looked up before MySQL removal is misleading.

Explicit constraint names can still be useful in products and contexts that support them as intended. The important maintenance rule is to inspect the actual engine representation. Do not infer removal syntax solely from the name written in a conceptual diagram or from a migration targeting another product. Syntax, catalog identity and the modeled business key are related but different roles.

## Key order has operational consequences without changing pair identity

For the same two required roles, uniqueness of the complete pair does not mean the engine stores or searches both column orders identically. Supporting index structures and access patterns can depend on component order. A query filtering one leading role can have different index usefulness from a query filtering only another role.

Choose and verify the actual physical definition against relevant workloads after the logical identity is correct. A three-row exercise cannot establish which index arrangement gives the best production latency. Likewise, a primary key does not guarantee the result display order of an unrestricted SELECT. Use ORDER BY when an assessment or user-facing report requires a deterministic presentation.

## Referenced keys create a dependency boundary

Foreign keys and application references can depend on the chosen identity. Replacing a primary key can therefore affect more than one table's local definition. A new surrogate key does not automatically rewrite every dependent reference or migrate external identifiers. Identify the referencing roles and their intended mapping before preparing a key transition.

MySQL may reject a key removal when the resulting definition would violate applicable dependency or AUTO_INCREMENT indexing requirements. Do not disable checks or remove references merely to make the statement succeed. A staged supported change needs its own data, compatibility and enforcement plan. The temporary key exercises do not claim to verify native persistent foreign-key transitions.

## A candidate key can remain unique without being primary

A table may have several valid candidate identities while designating one primary key. A required institutional code can remain protected by an appropriate unique rule when another key is primary. The distinction is useful for understanding why changing the primary designation does not necessarily require abandoning every other integrity invariant.

Conversely, dropping the primary constraint can weaken accepted state even if no row changes immediately. Later duplicates or missing values may become possible unless other rules still exclude them. The actual outcome depends on retained definitions. Review the whole final contract rather than assuming a key change affects only the visual label shown by a database browser.

## Keep conflict handling separate from key declaration

A rejected duplicate insert reveals that the protected identity already exists or conflicts under the selected rule. It does not prescribe a universal response. An application might treat a request as an idempotent retry, report a conflict or perform a defined update, but those policies require more information than the key error alone.

The exercises use ordinary writes and explicit rejected-input checks so the constraint remains visible. They do not add IGNORE, delete an old row or overwrite data to conceal a violation. That makes the table's accepted identity contract easier to learn before introducing upsert and concurrency topics with their own decision rules and failure cases.

## Exercise definitions and post-alter writes

The introductory task defines a composite primary key in a new temporary table and copies the supplied compatible enrollment pairs. The medium task adds that key to an existing candidate table without replacing its rows. Hidden cases include repeated components with different full pairs and an empty population, so the solution cannot assume one row per student or memorize the sample.

Separate negative cases attempt a duplicate complete pair and a missing key component. These test identity and required presence independently under the strict fixture settings. The expected ordered read verifies the preserved valid population. An empty output alone would not demonstrate that the key exists, so the rejected writes provide useful additional evidence about the actual definition.

## Report syntax and execution scope precisely

A complete key declaration explanation states the intended grain, every component, the allowed repetition of individual roles and the target's maintenance syntax. It also identifies generation and dependent references as separate concerns. Those details help the learner read both CREATE and ALTER forms without turning a convenient shorthand into an incorrect relational model.

Recorded MariaDB compatibility execution verifies the supplied temporary-table definitions and rejected writes. Exact MySQL/provider execution, production index performance and native persistent reference transitions remain separately unverified. The prepared content migrations store these instructional packages only; they do not apply the example key changes to application tables. Local assessment validity should not be mistaken for an authorized production identity migration.

questions.question_text: Why must a composite primary key spanning two columns be declared using table-level syntax?
options: Because column-level syntax cannot list more than one column at a time
Because MySQL disallows composite keys entirely
Because table-level syntax is faster to execute
Because composite keys require a separate CHECK constraint
questions.explanation: Column-level PRIMARY KEY syntax attaches inline to a single column definition and has no way to reference a second column, so any multi-column key must use the table-level PRIMARY KEY (col1, col2) clause.

questions.question_text: In MySQL, how do you drop the primary key from a table named students?
options: ALTER TABLE students DROP CONSTRAINT pk_students;
ALTER TABLE students DROP PRIMARY KEY;
ALTER TABLE students DROP KEY PRIMARY;
DROP PRIMARY KEY FROM students;
questions.explanation: MySQL provides a dedicated DROP PRIMARY KEY clause since it does not let you assign a custom name to the primary key; DROP CONSTRAINT is used in PostgreSQL/Oracle/SQL Server instead.

questions.question_text: What must be true of existing table data before ALTER TABLE ... ADD CONSTRAINT ... PRIMARY KEY (col) will succeed?
options: The column must already be indexed
The column must contain no NULLs and no duplicate values
The table must be empty
The column must be of an integer data type
questions.explanation: Adding a PRIMARY KEY validates existing rows: any NULL or duplicate value in the target column(s) causes the ALTER TABLE to fail.

questions.question_text: How many primary-key constraints may one table declaration contain?
options: Unlimited, one per candidate key
At most one, potentially over several columns
Up to two, for redundancy
As many as there are UNIQUE constraints
questions.explanation: A table may omit a primary-key declaration; multiple component columns do not mean multiple primary constraints.

questions.question_text: How should automatic numbering be distinguished from primary identity?
options: Yes, they cannot exist independently
Generation supplies values while a key constraint enforces identity, subject to engine-specific declaration requirements
Yes, but only in PostgreSQL
No, but only if the table has no other columns
questions.explanation: MySQL AUTO_INCREMENT indexing requirements still apply.

questions.question_text: What removal form identifies the primary key in MySQL?
options: The table cannot be queried until it is named
ALTER TABLE students DROP PRIMARY KEY;
The primary key silently becomes a UNIQUE constraint instead
Unnamed primary keys are rejected at CREATE TABLE time
questions.explanation: MySQL exposes the special PRIMARY key rather than requiring a guessed arbitrary generated constraint name.

questions.question_text: Which statement correctly declares a composite primary key on (student_id, course_id) for an existing empty table enrollments?
options: ALTER TABLE enrollments ADD PRIMARY KEY student_id, course_id;
ALTER TABLE enrollments ADD CONSTRAINT pk_enroll PRIMARY KEY (student_id, course_id);
ALTER TABLE enrollments MODIFY PRIMARY KEY (student_id) AND (course_id);
ALTER TABLE enrollments SET PRIMARY KEY = (student_id, course_id);
questions.explanation: The table-level ADD CONSTRAINT ... PRIMARY KEY (col1, col2) form is the correct portable syntax for adding a composite key to an existing table.

questions.question_text: If a table's primary key needs to change from one column to a different column entirely, what is generally required across most SQL engines?
options: A single ALTER TABLE RENAME PRIMARY KEY statement
Dropping the existing primary key constraint and adding a new one on the new column
Recreating the entire database
It cannot be done once data exists in the table
questions.explanation: There is no universal direct 'rename primary key column set' operation; the standard approach is DROP CONSTRAINT (or DROP PRIMARY KEY) followed by ADD CONSTRAINT ... PRIMARY KEY on the new column(s).

questions.question_text: Does PRIMARY KEY(student_id,course_id) forbid student 1 in two different courses?
options: Yes
No
Only with text ids
Only when named
questions.explanation: The whole pair defines the identity.

questions.question_text: Can two separate PRIMARY KEY clauses define one composite key?
options: Yes
Only with parentheses
No
Only on empty input
questions.explanation: List components in one supported declaration.

questions.question_text: Which pair duplicates accepted (1,10)?
questions.explanation: Complete-key repetition causes the conflict.

questions.question_text: Why test a NULL component after key addition?
options: To verify label sorting
To benchmark indexes
To create another key
To verify complete required identity
questions.explanation: Required components and uniqueness are distinct checks.

questions.question_text: Does a primary key guarantee SELECT display order?
options: No
Yes
Only for integers
Only with one component
questions.explanation: Presentation requires an explicit ordering contract.

questions.question_text: What must a surrogate enrollment_id not be assumed to enforce?
options: Its declared primary uniqueness
One accepted row per student-course pair unless another rule does so
Its nonmissing key rule
Its supplied definition
questions.explanation: Business pair uniqueness can be a separate invariant.

questions.question_text: Why review referenced tables before changing a key?
options: All references are rewritten automatically
Only note headings change
Dependent identities and accepted references may need a compatible transition
No other table can depend on a key
questions.explanation: Key transitions cross data-contract boundaries.

questions.question_text: Does DISTINCT in a report repair source-key violations?
options: Yes
Only with ORDER BY
Only for a composite key
No
questions.explanation: Query deduplication is not source enforcement.

questions.question_text: Can key component order affect index access usefulness?
options: Yes, under the actual physical definition and workload
No, under every engine
Only if aliases differ
Only if labels are unique
questions.explanation: Logical pair identity and index access are different questions.

questions.question_text: What should happen to compatible rows when adding the exercise key?
options: They receive invented ids
Their original values remain intact
They are deleted and recreated from one sample
Only the first row survives
questions.explanation: The task changes integrity definition, not the accepted population.

questions.question_text: Does dropping a primary key always succeed despite dependencies?
options: Yes
Only with a short name
No
Only in a transaction
questions.explanation: Applicable reference and indexing rules can block it.

questions.question_text: What does a duplicate-key error determine by itself?
options: An instruction to delete the old row
A mandate to ignore every error
A proof of external fraud
A protected identity conflict, not a universal application response
questions.explanation: Handling policy needs domain context.

coding_problems.title: Declare one composite primary identity for accepted enrollments
coding_problems.task: Create TEMPORARY current_enrollments with student_id INT NOT NULL,course_id INT NOT NULL and one PRIMARY KEY(student_id,course_id). Copy every supplied compatible pair from enrollment_input and return the pairs. Component values may repeat when the full pair differs.
coding_problems.schema_sql: SET SESSION sql_mode='STRICT_ALL_TABLES'; CREATE TABLE enrollment_input (student_id INT NOT NULL,course_id INT NOT NULL);
constraints: Every positive fixture has distinct complete nonmissing pairs.
edge_cases: Empty input still requires the key definition.
hints: List both roles in one table-level clause.
Do not add separate unique rules to each component.
coding_problems.solution_sql: CREATE TEMPORARY TABLE current_enrollments (student_id INT NOT NULL,course_id INT NOT NULL,PRIMARY KEY(student_id,course_id)); INSERT INTO current_enrollments SELECT student_id,course_id FROM enrollment_input; SELECT student_id,course_id FROM current_enrollments ORDER BY student_id,course_id;
coding_problems.explanation: The designated identity is the complete participation pair, not either component alone.

coding_problems.title: Add a primary key to compatible existing pairs
coding_problems.task: Add PRIMARY KEY(student_id,course_id) to candidate_enrollments using ALTER TABLE without replacing or changing its supplied rows. Every positive fixture is already compatible: complete pairs are distinct and nonmissing. Return all pairs. Do not resolve invalid data silently.
coding_problems.schema_sql: SET SESSION sql_mode='STRICT_ALL_TABLES'; CREATE TABLE candidate_enrollments (student_id INT NULL,course_id INT NULL);
constraints: Existing data is explicitly compatible with the proposed key.
The final rule requires complete identity.
edge_cases: Empty population still receives its key.
Subsequent duplicate and NULL writes are rejected.
hints: Use one composite PRIMARY KEY clause in ALTER TABLE.
Read back the unchanged pair population.
coding_problems.solution_sql: ALTER TABLE candidate_enrollments ADD PRIMARY KEY(student_id,course_id); SELECT student_id,course_id FROM candidate_enrollments ORDER BY student_id,course_id;
coding_problems.explanation: The alteration establishes the complete designated identity while preserving valid current facts.

original_questions.question_text: What is the naming convention risk of NOT explicitly naming a PRIMARY KEY constraint?

The engine auto-generates a name you must look up later before you can DROP CONSTRAINT by name
The primary key silently becomes a UNIQUE constraint instead
Unnamed primary keys are rejected at CREATE TABLE time
